title: Load Balancing
concept: Load balancing spreads requests across a pool of backends so that no single instance saturates. The hard parts are choosing which backends each client may talk to (subsetting), deciding where each request goes (round-robin, least-loaded, power of two choices), and reacting to load and health signals that are always slightly stale.

points: The hard parts are choosing which backends each client may talk to, deciding where each request goes, and reacting to load signals that are always slightly stale.
Uber found that a subsetting design needing no coordination between clients scales and fails more gracefully, and that subsets too large are safer than too small.
Dropbox found CPU alone looked healthy on servers stuck on disk I/O, so it balances on the higher of CPU and in-flight requests.

prerequisiteReasons.dns: Load balancing takes from DNS the idea of one name that stands for many servers, and the staleness of answers that clients keep using.
prerequisiteReasons.http-tcp-tls: Balancing at the transport layer or the application layer only makes sense once you know what a TCP connection and an HTTP request are, and what each costs.

posts.title: Better Load Balancing: Real-Time Dynamic Subsetting

digest.problem: In Uber's service mesh, each host's proxy connects to only a subset of a backend service's tasks, chosen at random, and that subset had a fixed size. Callers sending heavy traffic squeezed it through the same small subset as quiet callers, so some backend tasks ran hot while others sat idle. Each case was fixed by hand-tuning subset sizes, and the right size kept drifting as traffic changed.
digest.constraints: The mesh spans thousands of services in millions of containers, with services from tens to tens of thousands of tasks and traffic that can swing from 100 to 100,000 requests per second within minutes. Fully connecting two 10,000-task services would need about 100,000,000 connections. One proxy is shared by every task on a host and must be ready for any destination. The fix had to reuse the existing control plane and load reports, avoid reserving capacity per service, The chosen design kept task selection random, with no coordination between proxies.

walkthrough.explanation: Each proxy periodically reports how much traffic it sends to each destination service.
Aggregators combine the reports, and a few global controllers build a view of total traffic per service.
The total for each service is pushed back to every proxy within seconds. It does not need to be perfectly consistent across the fleet.
Each proxy compares its own smoothed traffic to a service with that service's total and sizes its subset in proportion, so a proxy carrying a bigger share connects to more of the service's tasks.
A tunable constant scales the result, with a minimum subset size for quiet callers and a cap on total connections.
Which tasks go in the subset is still random, so proxies never need to coordinate.

tradeoffs.chosen: Subset size computed per proxy from its share of total traffic, with random task selection and no coordination between proxies.
tradeoffs.rejected: Fixed subset sizes with manual tuning, and least-pending-request balancing alone, which helped too little. Considered but not built: deterministic subsets that need proxies to coordinate, and tracking load per caller or procedure.
tradeoffs.why: Reusing load reports the control plane already had made the fix cheap to build, and keeping proxies independent kept it simple and resilient. The price is a few seconds of lag, some leftover imbalance from random picks, and more connections per proxy, which they capped.

digest.failures: Static subsets had already failed for the largest services, and least-pending-request balancing helped too little because each proxy only knew about its own requests. Months after rollout, during a protocol migration, a few hosts running many busy callers against large pools opened thousands of connections and hit a memory problem in Go's HTTP/2 code; capping connections fixed it. The first scaling constant was picked fairly arbitrarily and raised a year later once they could measure better.
digest.takeaways: Look for signals the system already collects before building new ones. A design that needs no coordination between clients scales and fails more gracefully. Erring toward subsets that are too large is safer than too small. Record a baseline before a fleet-wide rollout, because gains are hard to prove afterwards.

posts.title: What’s new with Robinhood, our in-house load balancing service

digest.problem: Dropbox clients spread requests round-robin across the servers they knew about, with no idea how busy each one was. The fleet mixes hardware generations, so the same request costs more on some machines than others, and some servers overloaded while others idled.
digest.constraints: Some services have millions of clients, so each client only talks to a subset of servers. Clients use both Envoy and gRPC, and client changes take months to reach everyone because some clients rarely deploy. The system also had to survive restarts, new servers, missing load reports, and traffic split across data centers, and the move off the old strategy had to be gradual.

walkthrough.explanation: Servers send load reports through a per-data-center proxy to a load balancing service that is sharded by the service being balanced.
For each server, a PID controller compares its utilization with the service's average and nudges that server's weight up or down.
Weights are normalized across the service and stored in a ZooKeeper or etcd-based routing database, which pushes changes to anyone watching.
Clients receive weights through Envoy's endpoint discovery and do weighted round-robin. For gRPC, Dropbox wrote its own picker based on earliest-deadline-first scheduling.
A locality config sets how much traffic each zone sends to each other zone, so clients pick a zone first and a server second.
After a restart, controller state is restored from the routing database; new servers start at a low weight; if 15% of load reports are missing, the update is skipped.

tradeoffs.chosen: A central service that sets per-server weights from measured utilization, with clients doing weighted round-robin.
tradeoffs.rejected: Server load in response headers with clients choosing the least loaded server, larger subsets as a tuning knob, and balancing on CPU alone.
tradeoffs.why: Logic in one central service can change and roll back in minutes, while client changes take months. The cost is a feedback loop that needs steady traffic, so very quiet services and requests that take minutes balance poorly.

digest.failures: The header-based approach worked but needed code changes on every server and client and was hard to roll out everywhere. Servers with stalled disk I/O showed low CPU, so the controller kept sending them more traffic; they now balance on the higher of CPU and in-flight requests. The migration process was not well designed from the start, so Dropbox spent much more time than expected reimplementing it and redesigning the configuration.
digest.takeaways: Keep configuration minimal with good defaults. Put logic where it can be changed and rolled back fastest. Dropbox found that CPU alone can look healthy on a stuck server, so it uses the higher of CPU and in-flight requests. Plan the migration while designing the system, and count migration effort as part of the cost.

comparison:
Uber and Dropbox started from the same problem: clients spreading requests over a subset of servers still left some servers running much hotter than others.

Uber changed who each proxy talks to, resizing its subset in near real time from load reports gathered by the control plane, so a caller that sends more traffic spreads it over more backends.

Dropbox decided that tuning subset size only added another knob and instead changed how much traffic each server gets, with weights driven by measured utilization, which absorbs its mix of hardware generations and keeps the logic in one central service rather than in every client.

glossary.definition: The slice of a service's servers that one client is allowed to connect to.
Sending each new request to the next server in a list, in turn.
Round-robin where servers with higher weights receive proportionally more requests.
The value below which 99% of measurements fall, used to describe the slow or busy tail.
The part of a system that computes and distributes configuration, as opposed to the data plane that carries requests.
A feedback loop that adjusts an output based on the current error, its accumulation over time, and how fast it is changing.

mistakes: Assuming round-robin spreads load evenly. It spreads requests evenly, but requests differ in cost and servers differ in hardware, so load does not.
Balancing on a signal that can look healthy while the server is stuck, such as CPU on a server waiting on slow disks.
Letting every client connect to every server. Connection counts grow with clients times servers, so at scale each client needs a bounded subset.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why a service needs a load balancer once it runs on more than one server.
why.body:
DNS can give out several addresses for a name, but resolvers cache answers for the length of the TTL, so DNS cannot react when one server is overloaded or down. Something closer to the traffic has to make a fresh choice for each connection or request.

That choice decides whether the fleet is used well. If some servers run hot while others sit idle, the hot ones get slow, and teams buy extra capacity just to stay safe. A good load balancer keeps every server about equally busy, so the fleet can be smaller and still handle the peaks.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture who decides where a request goes and what information they use.
mentalModel.body:
Think of a load balancer as a dispatcher between callers and a pool of identical servers. For each connection or request it answers one question: which server now? It can answer blindly, in turn, which is round-robin, or using what it knows about each server's load and health.

Two things make this harder than it sounds. The load it sees is always a little out of date, because reports take time to arrive. And at scale no caller can connect to every server, so each caller only talks to a subset, and the balancer can only spread work within that subset.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through how a request is routed and how the balancer learns about load.

steps.explanation: Each caller, or the proxy beside it, connects to a bounded set of the service's servers instead of all of them, because connection counts grow with callers times servers.
Within the subset, a rule picks the server: in turn (round-robin), in proportion to weights (weighted round-robin), or by comparing load.
Servers or proxies report how busy they are, for example CPU, requests in flight, or traffic sent.
A control plane turns those reports into new subset sizes or new weights and pushes them out. The data is a few seconds old when it is used.
Health checks take failing servers out of rotation and bring them back when they recover.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can follow how two companies evened out load on real fleets.

steps.explanation: At Dropbox, clients sent requests round-robin over the servers they knew. Because the fleet mixed hardware generations, the same request cost more on some machines, and the busiest server in a database frontend cluster ran at 1.4 times the average CPU.
Dropbox's Robinhood service collects load reports and runs a controller per server that nudges its weight up when it is less busy than average and down when it is busier.
Weights go into a routing database that pushes changes to clients, which then do weighted round-robin. The busiest server dropped to 1.05 times the average.
Servers with stalled disks showed low CPU and kept getting more traffic, so Robinhood now balances on the higher of CPU and requests in flight.

Uber attacked the same problem from the other side. Busy callers squeezed their traffic through the same fixed-size subset as quiet callers, so each proxy now sizes its subset from its share of the service's total traffic.
Uber's proxies already reported traffic per destination, so the control plane sent the totals back within seconds. Of the 36 last-onboarded power services, 17 saw p99 CPU fall by 10% or more.

lesson.mistakesOutcome: After this you can avoid three ways load balancing goes wrong.
lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: Why can't DNS alone keep servers evenly loaded?
options: It can only return one address
It does not work inside a data center
Resolvers cache its answers, so it cannot react quickly to one server being busy or down
quiz.why: DNS answers are reused until their TTL runs out, so a change in load is not seen in time.
wrong: DNS can return several addresses for one name.
Where DNS runs is not the issue; caching is.

quiz.question: Round-robin sends the same number of requests to each server. Why can load still be uneven?
options: Requests differ in cost and servers differ in hardware
Round-robin skips servers at random whenever one of them looks busy
It only works with two servers, so larger pools fall back to random choice
quiz.why: Equal request counts are not equal work when some requests or machines are more expensive.
wrong: Round-robin takes servers strictly in turn.
It works with any number of servers.

quiz.question: Why does each caller connect to only a subset of servers at scale?
options: Subsets are faster to encrypt because each connection carries fewer handshakes
Connecting everyone to everyone needs callers times servers connections
Servers can only accept one caller at a time, so callers are split into groups
quiz.why: Two services with 10,000 tasks each would need on the order of 100 million connections if fully meshed.
wrong: Encryption has nothing to do with it.
Servers accept many callers; the total connection count is the problem.

quiz.question: A server's disk stalls. Its CPU drops and the balancer sends it more traffic. What went wrong?
options: Round-robin was turned off, so the balancer fell back to sending extra traffic to idle servers
The subset was too large, so the server was picked by more callers than it could take
The balancer used a load signal that looks healthy while the server is stuck
quiz.why: Low CPU looked like spare capacity. Adding requests in flight to the signal shows the server is actually stuck.
wrong: The problem was the signal, not the rule.
Subset size does not change what the signal reports.

quiz.question: Load reports reach the balancer a few seconds late. What does that mean in practice?
options: Decisions are made on slightly stale data, so the system must tolerate some lag and imbalance
Reports must be sent on every request
quiz.why: Every balancer works from data that is a little old; good designs smooth it and accept a few seconds of lag.
wrong: Real systems balance well with stale data, as long as they expect it.
Per-request reporting would cost more than it saves.

quiz.question: What does weighted round-robin do?
options: Sends each server traffic in proportion to its weight
Picks a server at random, then adjusts the odds after each response arrives
Sends everything to the heaviest server until it is full, then moves to the next one
quiz.why: Higher-weight servers get more turns, so a controller can shift load by changing weights.
wrong: It is deterministic in proportion, not random.
Weights share traffic out; they do not send it all to one server.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies fixed uneven load, one by resizing subsets and one by weighting servers.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain when to change who a caller talks to and when to change how much each server gets.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a fleet, design a balancer, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: Your service runs on two hardware generations and the older servers are always the hottest, even with round-robin. What do you change?
exercises.answer: Give each server a weight and adjust it from measured load, so older servers get fewer requests. Use a signal such as the higher of CPU and requests in flight, so a stuck server cannot look idle.
exercises.tradeoffs: Weights need a feedback loop and steady traffic to work well, and a bad signal can push traffic to the wrong place.
wrongAnswers: Adding more servers of both kinds and keeping round-robin.
Assuming equal request counts mean equal load.

exercises.prompt: Design a load balancer for a service with tens of thousands of callers and a few thousand servers.
exercises.answer: Give each caller a bounded random subset, collect load reports in a central service, turn them into weights or subset sizes, and push those out. Clients do weighted round-robin within their subset. Keep the logic central so it can change in minutes, and handle missing reports, restarts and new servers explicitly.
exercises.tradeoffs: Central logic is easy to change but adds a dependency and a few seconds of lag; changes in clients can take months to roll out.
wrongAnswers: Full mesh between every caller and server.
Logic that only lives in clients and needs every client to redeploy.
No plan for missing load reports.

exercises.prompt: Traffic grows ten times and a few callers now send most of it. What breaks and what do you do?
exercises.answer: Fixed subsets put heavy callers on too few servers. Size each caller's subset from its share of total traffic, with a minimum for quiet callers and a cap on connections per proxy, and record a baseline before rolling out so you can prove the gain.
exercises.tradeoffs: Bigger subsets mean more connections and memory per proxy, so the cap matters; too small is worse than too large.
wrongAnswers: Raising one global subset size for everyone.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: Once requests spread evenly across many servers, those servers still read from shared databases, often the same data again and again. Caching picks up from there: serving repeated reads from memory, and keeping those copies correct. Three later topics build on it as well: Capacity, on how many servers should sit behind the balancer and how fast to add or remove them, Safe Deployments, on moving traffic to new code in small steps, and Overload and Cascading Failures, on what happens when one server's failure shifts its load onto the rest.
